title: Preprocessor macros & #define for CP

hook.scenario: You define a macro to square a number: `#define SQ(x) x * x`. When you calculate `SQ(3 + 2)`, you expect 25, but your program outputs 11.
hook.question: Why did a simple arithmetic macro give the wrong answer?

mental_model.intuition: The preprocessor is like a mindless find-and-replace tool running in Microsoft Word before your code even reaches the compiler. It knows nothing about C++ syntax, types, or order of operations.
mental_model.description: Macros (`#define`) are processed before compilation. They perform naive text substitution. If you write `#define SQ(x) x * x` and call `SQ(3 + 2)`, the preprocessor replaces it literally with `3 + 2 * 3 + 2`. Due to operator precedence, this evaluates to `3 + 6 + 2 = 11`. To fix this, you must aggressively parenthesize macro arguments. Better yet, in modern C++, avoid macros and use `constexpr` or `inline` functions instead.

explanation:
In Competitive Programming (CP), macros are heavily used to save typing (e.g., `#define pb push_back` or `#define rep(i, a, b) for(int i=a; i<b; ++i)`). However, they are inherently dangerous because they don't obey C++ scoping rules or type checking.

When you use macros for expressions, you must wrap every argument in parentheses, and the entire expression in parentheses: `#define SQ(x) ((x) * (x))`. Without this, operator precedence will ruin expressions like `SQ(a+b)` or `100 / SQ(5)`.

Furthermore, macros can cause 'double-evaluation' bugs. If you call `SQ(i++)`, it expands to `((i++) * (i++))`, incrementing `i` twice and invoking undefined behaviour.

In modern software engineering (SWE), macros are strongly discouraged except for conditional compilation (`#ifdef`). You should use `constexpr` functions (which are typed, scoped, and evaluated at compile-time if possible) or `const` variables instead.

code_snippets.title: The bug: Naive text substitution
code_snippets.explanation: Because the preprocessor just blindly pastes text, the C++ compiler receives an expression with standard operator precedence. Multiplication happens before addition, destroying the intended logic.

code_snippets.title: The fix: Parentheses or constexpr
code_snippets.explanation: Aggressive parentheses fix the precedence issues, but macros still suffer from double-evaluation if you pass an expression with side effects. `constexpr` functions solve all these problems by acting as real, type-safe C++ functions.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting the outer parentheses
common_mistakes.explanation: Writing `#define ADD(a, b) (a) + (b)` fails if you do `10 * ADD(2, 3)`. It expands to `10 * (2) + (3) == 23`, not 50. You need `#define ADD(a, b) ((a) + (b))`.

common_mistakes.title: Passing increments to macros
common_mistakes.explanation: Never pass `i++` or `++i` to a macro like `MAX(a, b)` because the macro might expand it multiple times, e.g., `((a++) > (b) ? (a++) : (b))`.

recall_questions.q: Why does #define SQ(x) x * x fail for SQ(3 + 2)?
recall_questions.answer: Macros perform literal text replacement before compilation. It expands to 3 + 2 * 3 + 2, which evaluates to 11 due to operator precedence, instead of the expected 25.

recall_questions.q: How do you properly write a macro that evaluates an expression?
recall_questions.answer: You must wrap every instance of the arguments in parentheses, and wrap the entire macro definition in parentheses, e.g., #define SQ(x) ((x) * (x)).

recall_questions.q: What is the modern C++ alternative to macro functions and why is it better?
recall_questions.answer: constexpr or inline functions. They are type-safe, obey scope rules, avoid double-evaluation bugs (like passing i++), and can still be evaluated at compile time.

oa_questions.question: A candidate's code contains `#define MAX(a, b) a > b ? a : b`. They use it as `int ans = MAX(x, y) + 5;`. Why is this a bug and how do you fix it?
oa_questions.answer: It expands to `x > y ? x : y + 5`. Because `+` has higher precedence than `? :`, it evaluates as `x > y ? x : (y + 5)`. The fix is `#define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))`.
oa_questions.approach: Identify the lack of outer parentheses and the precedence of the ternary operator.

oa_questions.question: Why is `#define PI 3.14159` considered bad practice in modern C++?
oa_questions.answer: Macros do not respect scope (they leak everywhere) and have no type. The modern, type-safe alternative is `constexpr double PI = 3.14159;` inside a namespace.
oa_questions.approach: Compare macros to modern compile-time constants.

key_points.title: Parenthesize everything
key_points.detail: If you must write a macro, wrap every argument and the whole expression in `()`.

key_points.title: Prefer constexpr
key_points.detail: In SWE, replace macro constants with `constexpr int` and macro functions with `constexpr` functions.
